story_type: space shuttle lands in a desert crosswind with missing tiles and pops a wheelie, 1982 crew film
hook: A space shuttle popped a wheelie on a desert runway.
narration: A space shuttle popped a wheelie on a desert runway.
March 1982. Columbia launched on the third shuttle flight, with Jack Lousma and Gordon Fullerton.
On day two they saw a problem. Tiles were missing in front of the windshield.
Those tiles shield the shuttle from the heat of reentry, so every gap matters.
They swung the robot arm around for a better look and found more missing.
When it was time to come home, Mission Control waved them off for a day.
Then Columbia fell from twenty five times the speed of sound to a stop in about half an hour.
A strong westerly wind pushed them sideways. Crabbing into it hid the runway from view.
They aimed for a rectangle marked on the white sand.
[short pause] The nose wheel came down too fast. Holding it up, the pilot over rotated, and the nose popped back into the air.
outcome: Columbia settled back down and rolled out smoothly at White Sands, with no harm done.
title: Space shuttle popped a wheelie
description:
In March 1982, on shuttle flight STS-3, Columbia flew with tiles missing near the windshield, then landed in a strong crosswind on the Northrup Strip at White Sands, where the nose popped back up before the rollout. From the crew's own post flight film.

Footage: NASA video (STS-3 Mission Highlights, 1982), via Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:STS-3_Mission_Highlights.webm

facts.source_quote: Launch: March 22, 1982. Crew: Jack Lousma, Gordon Fullerton. Vehicle: Columbia.

facts.claim: Day two, tiles missing in front of windshield
facts.source_quote: And Jack had discovered some tile missing out in front of the windshield.
So we moved the arm up and got it over to the right hand side and looked along on a kind of a grazing angle here,
but had a view and found some more tile missing.
So we got the payload bay doors closed and got a wave off for mission control.

facts.claim: Mach 25 to zero in 25 to 30 minutes
facts.source_quote: It was a machine that slowed down from 25 times a speed of sound to zero in about 25 to 30 minutes.
But because of the strong westerly wind we have a crab to the right.
But with that correction for the wind drift it's hiding the view of the runway.
We are actually aiming for the rectangle

facts.claim: Nose wheel, over rotated, wheelie, no harm
facts.source_quote: I noticed that the wheel nose wheel was going down a little more quickly than I wanted it to and had to hold it out some and doing so I over rotated a little bit kind of popped the wheelie there but no harm done.
And the Columbia made a good smooth rollout
landing at Holloman Air Force at White Sands Northrop Strip there.
